issues: The paper contradicts itself. The '201 hours' in its Discussion and Conclusions section matches neither its tables nor its own arithmetic. Table 7 gives a point estimate of 244 hours a year per user to read (range 181-304) and 154 hours to skim. The text says 'using the point estimate of 244 hours per year to read privacy policies per person means an average of 40 minutes a day'.

The $3,534 that the record pairs with 201 hours is actually computed from 244 hours. Table 8 splits it as work $2,791 at $35.86/hour plus home $743 at $4.48/hour, which is 243.7 hours. The national totals rest on the same figure: 221 million users x $3,534 = $781 billion, and 53.8 billion hours / 221 million = 243 hours. The published I/S version (4 I/S 543) has the same inconsistency. The numbers slice (mcdonald-cranor-hours-per-year-reading-privacy-policies) already uses 244.
The notes said 201 hours assumes word-for-word reading, but the paper's word-for-word point estimate is 244 hours.

fieldFixes.notes: Model estimate, not a measurement. It assumes each American internet user reads, word for word, the privacy policy of every site visited, once a year. Point estimate from the paper's Table 7: 244 hours to read (range 181-304) and 154 hours to skim, about 40 minutes a day. At 25% of wages for time at home and twice wages for time at work, this is worth about $3,534 per user per year. The paper's abstract and conclusion give 'approximately 201 hours a year, worth about $3,534', but 201 hours matches neither its tables nor its $3,534 and $781 billion figures, which are built on 244 hours.
